newsitem.title: USA: Fed seeks to cut money laundering at private banks.
newsitem.headline: Fed seeks to cut money laundering at private banks.

text.p: The Federal Reserve Board issued guidelines Wednesday to crack down on private banking departments that may be allowing wealthy individuals to evade anti-money laundering regulations.

The moves follows growing concern among law enforcement agencies and Congress that lax oversight in private banking, departments within banks that cater to the wealthiest bank depositors, may be facilitating illicit money transfers.
The new guidelines resulted from a yearlong review by the Fed of private bank operations at 40 U.S. and foreign banks that found problems at only a few institutions.
"To varying degrees, the sound practices identified here either are currently in place or are in the process of being implemented in most institutions," the Fed said.

Banks offer wealthy clients a host of personalized services through private banking, including money management, financial advice and investment transactions. But in some cases, banks may have evaded anti-money laundering rules in their zeal to cater to the needs of important customers.
Unde the Bank Secrecy Act, banks are required to report to the government all transfers over $10,000. Banks also are required to report "suspicious" transfers.

Private banks came under close scrutiny after revelations last year that Raul Salinas, brother of former Mexican President Carlos Salinas, may have used a private account at Citibank to move tens of millions of dollars out of Mexico to Swiss banks.
Citibank said its own investigation turned up no evidence that any laws were violated in handling the Salinas funds, but the Justice Department subsequently opened an investigation into the matter.
Congress has also raised concerns about private banking. Earlier this year, Representative Spencer Bachus, Republican of Alabama, asked the General Accounting Office to research the issue.
The 16-page Fed guidelines require banks to monitor private banking for suspicious transactions, perform basic background checks on customers and document any rules waived for such accounts.
Senior management should actively oversee private banking departments and create an "appropriate corporate culture," the Fed said.
